title: Matrix algebra, inverses, Invertible Matrix Theorem
summary: The algebra of matrices (with its non-commutative traps), how to compute and use inverses, elementary matrices, and the Invertible Matrix Theorem, which ties together everything from systems, independence and spanning for square matrices.

blocks.text: Entrywise, for matrices of the same size. The usual rules hold: A + B = B + A, (A + B) + C = A + (B + C), r(A + B) = rA + rB.
If A is m×n and B = [b₁ ⋯ bₚ] is n×p, then AB = [Ab₁ ⋯ Abₚ], an m×p matrix. Entry (i, j) = (row i of A)·(column j of B). Defined only when the inner sizes match.
Why this definition: AB is the matrix of the composition 'first B, then A', i.e. A(Bx) = (AB)x. Composition is associative, so A(BC) = (AB)C, but order matters.

blocks.name: Rules that hold
blocks.text: A(BC) = (AB)C; A(B + C) = AB + AC; (B + C)A = BA + CA; r(AB) = (rA)B = A(rB); IₘA = A = AIₙ.
Rules that FAIL: (1) AB ≠ BA in general. (2) AB = AC does not imply B = C. (3) AB = 0 does not imply A = 0 or B = 0. (4) (A + B)² ≠ A² + 2AB + B² unless AB = BA.
Aᵀ has rows = columns of A. Rules: (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A, (A + B)ᵀ = Aᵀ + Bᵀ, (rA)ᵀ = rAᵀ, and (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ (reverse order).

blocks.title: Non-commutativity and failed cancellation
blocks.prompt: Let A = [2 −3; −4 6], B = [8 4; 5 5], C = [5 −2; 3 1]. Compute AB, AC and BA.
steps: So AB = AC with B ≠ C, and AB ≠ BA. Cancellation fails because A is not invertible (its columns are parallel).

blocks.name: Why (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ
blocks.text: Entry (i, j) of (AB)ᵀ is entry (j, i) of AB = (row j of A)·(column i of B) = (column i of B)·(row j of A) = (row i of Bᵀ)·(column j of Aᵀ) = entry (i, j) of BᵀAᵀ.

blocks.name: Powers
blocks.text: Aᵏ = A·A⋯A (k factors) for square A, A⁰ = I. AʲAᵏ = Aʲ⁺ᵏ. But (AB)ᵏ ≠ AᵏBᵏ in general.

blocks.title: Algebra identities that fail (exam-hard twist)
blocks.prompt: With A = [1 2; 0 1] and B = [1 0; 1 1], compare (A + B)² with A² + 2AB + B², and (A + B)(A − B) with A² − B².
steps: The difference is AB − BA: (A + B)² = A² + AB + BA + B², which equals A² + 2AB + B² only if AB = BA.

blocks.text: An n×n matrix A is invertible if there is C with CA = I and AC = I. Then C = A⁻¹ is unique. A non-invertible matrix is called singular.

blocks.name: 2×2 inverse
blocks.text: A = [a b; c d] is invertible iff ad − bc ≠ 0, and then A⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc))·[d −b; −c a].

proof.text: Multiply out: [a b; c d][d −b; −c a] = (ad − bc)I.

blocks.name: Properties
blocks.text: If A is invertible, Ax = b has the unique solution x = A⁻¹b. (A⁻¹)⁻¹ = A. (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹. (Aᵀ)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)ᵀ.

proof.text: (AB)(B⁻¹A⁻¹) = A(BB⁻¹)A⁻¹ = AA⁻¹ = I: socks and shoes, undo in reverse order.

blocks.name: Algorithm
blocks.text: Row reduce [A | I]. If A reduces to I, the result is [I | A⁻¹]. If A does not reduce to I, A is not invertible.

proof.text: Each row operation is left multiplication by an elementary matrix. If Eₖ⋯E₁A = I then Eₖ⋯E₁ = A⁻¹, and the same operations turn I into Eₖ⋯E₁I = A⁻¹.

blocks.title: 2×2 formula
steps: Check row 1 of A times column 1: 3(−3) + 4(5/2) = 1. ✓

blocks.title: Inverse by row reducing [A | I]
steps: Left block is I, so the right block is A⁻¹.

blocks.name: The inverse is unique
blocks.text: If B and C are both inverses of A, then B = C.

blocks.name: Invertible ⇒ unique solution
blocks.text: If A is invertible, A x = b has exactly one solution, x = A⁻¹b.

proof.text: Existence: A(A⁻¹b) = b. Uniqueness: if Au = b then u = A⁻¹(Au) = A⁻¹b.

blocks.title: Inverse with a parameter (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: For which k is A = [1 k; k 4] invertible? Give A⁻¹ in terms of k.

blocks.title: When the algorithm detects singularity
blocks.prompt: Try to invert A = [1 2 3; 2 4 7; 3 6 10] by row reducing [A | I].
steps: The left block now has a zero row: A cannot be reduced to I. Column 2 = 2·column 1, so the columns are dependent.

blocks.text: If a zero row appears in the left block, stop: A is singular. Do not try to 'divide by zero' to keep going.
Treat matrices like numbers except: you may only multiply both sides on the same side, and only invertible matrices can be 'divided out'.

blocks.title: Recipe for solving for X
items: Undo outer inverses first using (PQ)⁻¹ = Q⁻¹P⁻¹.
Left-multiply by the inverse of the leftmost known factor; right-multiply by the inverse of the rightmost.
Simplify, then check by substituting back.

blocks.title: Solve AXB = C
blocks.prompt: With A = [1 2; 1 3], B = [2 1; 1 1], C = [4 1; 5 2], solve AXB = C for X.
steps: Left-multiply by A⁻¹ and right-multiply by B⁻¹: X = A⁻¹CB⁻¹ (not A⁻¹B⁻¹C!).

blocks.title: Symbolic matrix equation
blocks.prompt: A, B, C, X are invertible n×n with (B⁻¹XA)⁻¹ = CB. Solve for X.
steps: Right-multiply by B⁻¹: A⁻¹X⁻¹ = C. Left-multiply by A: X⁻¹ = AC.

blocks.text: (PQ)⁻¹ = P⁻¹Q⁻¹ is wrong (order reverses), and you cannot 'cancel' a factor that is not at the very left or very right.

blocks.title: Matrix equation with X on both sides (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: Solve AX = X + B for X, where A = [3 1; 1 2] and B = [1 1; 0 2]. What must be true for a unique solution?
steps: Move all X terms to one side: AX − X = B, i.e. (A − I)X = B. (Write X = IX before factoring: 'A − 1' is meaningless.)
Unique solution iff A − I is invertible. A − I = [2 1; 1 1], det = 1, (A − I)⁻¹ = [1 −1; −1 2].

blocks.text: Factor on the correct side: AX − X = (A − I)X, but XA − X = X(A − I). Mixing the sides is a common error.
A matrix obtained by performing ONE row operation on I. Multiplying EA performs that same row operation on A.

blocks.name: Inverses
blocks.text: Every elementary matrix is invertible; its inverse is the elementary matrix of the reverse operation (subtract instead of add, swap again, scale by 1/c).

blocks.name: Invertible = product of elementaries
blocks.text: A is invertible ⇔ A is row equivalent to I ⇔ A is a product of elementary matrices.

blocks.title: What an elementary matrix does
blocks.prompt: E = [1 0 0; 0 1 0; −4 0 1]. What does EA do to a 3×n matrix A? What is E⁻¹?
steps: E came from I by R₃ − 4R₁, so EA replaces row 3 of A by (row 3 − 4·row 1).
blocks.answer: EA performs R₃ − 4R₁ on A; E⁻¹ = [1 0 0; 0 1 0; 4 0 1].

blocks.text: To get the elementary matrix for a row operation, just do that operation to I. Swap matrices are their own inverses.

blocks.title: Write A and A⁻¹ as products of elementary matrices (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: Reduce A = [1 2; 3 4] to I, record elementary matrices, and express A⁻¹ and A as products.
steps: And A = E₁⁻¹E₂⁻¹E₃⁻¹ = [1 0; 3 1][1 0; 0 −2][1 2; 0 1] (the inverses in reverse order).

blocks.text: Row operations act on the left (EA); column operations act on the right (AE). This is why the [A | I] algorithm uses row operations only.

blocks.name: Invertible Matrix Theorem (square A, n×n)
blocks.text: The following are all true or all false: (a) A is invertible. (b) A is row equivalent to Iₙ. (c) A has n pivot positions. (d) Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution. (e) The columns of A are linearly independent. (f) x ↦ Ax is one-to-one. (g) Ax = b has at least one solution for every b. (h) The columns span ℝⁿ. (i) x ↦ Ax is onto. (j) There is C with CA = I. (k) There is D with AD = I. (l) Aᵀ is invertible. Later additions: det A ≠ 0; 0 is not an eigenvalue; Col A = ℝⁿ; rank A = n; Nul A = {0}.

proof.text: The engine: for a SQUARE matrix, 'pivot in every column' (uniqueness side: d, e, f) and 'pivot in every row' (existence side: g, h, i) both say 'n pivots'. So one-to-one ⇔ onto.

blocks.name: One-sided inverses suffice
blocks.text: If A, B are square and AB = I, then BA = I and B = A⁻¹.

proof.text: AB = I ⇒ Ax = b is solvable for every b (take x = Bb) ⇒ by the IMT A is invertible. Then B = A⁻¹(AB) = A⁻¹, so BA = A⁻¹A = I.

blocks.text: The IMT is only for square matrices. A 3×2 A and a 2×3 B can have BA = I₂ while AB is singular.

blocks.title: IMT chain
blocks.prompt: A is 5×5 and Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution. List five other facts that follow. Then: what if instead Ax = b fails to be consistent for some b?
steps: Only the trivial solution ⇒ pivot in every column ⇒ (square) 5 pivots.
Hence: A is invertible; A ~ I₅; columns are independent and span ℝ⁵; x ↦ Ax is one-to-one and onto; Ax = b has exactly one solution for every b; Aᵀ is invertible; det A ≠ 0.

If Ax = b is inconsistent for some b, the columns don't span ℝ⁵, so fewer than 5 pivots: A is singular, Ax = 0 has nontrivial solutions, the columns are dependent, the map is not one-to-one, det A = 0. All the IMT conditions fail together.
blocks.answer: All IMT conditions hold together (invertible, independent columns, spanning columns, one-to-one, onto, det ≠ 0…), or all fail together.

blocks.text: T: ℝⁿ → ℝⁿ is invertible if there is S with S(T(x)) = x and T(S(x)) = x. T(x) = Ax is invertible iff A is, and then S(x) = A⁻¹x.

blocks.title: IMT from indirect information (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: A is 4×4 and Ae₁ = Ae₂ (columns 1 and 2 are equal). What can you say about det A, Nul A, Col A, and the number of solutions of Ax = b?
steps: A(e₁ − e₂) = 0 with e₁ − e₂ ≠ 0: Ax = 0 has a nontrivial solution.
By the IMT, A is singular: det A = 0, fewer than 4 pivots, columns dependent and not spanning ℝ⁴, Col A ≠ ℝ⁴.
Nul A contains (1, −1, 0, 0), so dim Nul A ≥ 1.
For each b: if b ∉ Col A there is no solution; if b ∈ Col A there are infinitely many (a free variable). Never exactly one.
blocks.answer: Singular: det A = 0, Nul A ≠ {0}, Col A ≠ ℝ⁴; Ax = b has either no solution or infinitely many.

blocks.text: Invertible linear transformations: T(x) = Ax is invertible iff A is; then T⁻¹(x) = A⁻¹x. For square A, one-to-one and onto are equivalent, so 'T is one-to-one' alone already makes T invertible. For non-square A neither direction can give invertibility.

blocks.title: Six True/False
blocks.prompt: (a) If AB = I for square A, B, then BA = I. (b) If A² = 0 then A = 0. (c) (A + B)⁻¹ = A⁻¹ + B⁻¹. (d) If A is invertible, so is Aᵀ. (e) If the columns of a square A span ℝⁿ, then Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution. (f) If AB is invertible (A, B square), then B is invertible.
steps: (a) True: one-sided inverse of a square matrix is two-sided (IMT).
(c) False: A = B = I gives (2I)⁻¹ = ½I ≠ 2I.
(f) True: ((AB)⁻¹A)B = I, so B has a left inverse, hence is invertible.
blocks.answer: (a) T (b) F (c) F (d) T (e) T (f) T

blocks.text: Standard counterexample stock: [0 1; 0 0] (nilpotent), [1 0; 0 0] (projection), −I, and two 2×2 matrices with AB = 0 like [1 0; 0 0] and [0 0; 1 0].

In practice A⁻¹ is rarely the fastest way to solve one system (row reducing [A | b] is cheaper), but it pays off when the same A meets many right-hand sides, and A⁻¹ formulas are essential for theory and for 2×2 work by hand.

blocks.title: Several systems with the same coefficient matrix
blocks.prompt: Solve Ax = b₁ and Ax = b₂ for A = [2 5; 1 3], b₁ = (1, 2), b₂ = (4, −1).
steps: Equivalently, row reduce [A | b₁ b₂] once: both columns are processed together.

blocks.name: Diagonal and triangular inverses
blocks.text: A diagonal matrix is invertible iff all diagonal entries are nonzero, and then its inverse is diagonal with the reciprocals. An invertible upper (lower) triangular matrix has an upper (lower) triangular inverse whose diagonal entries are the reciprocals of the original ones.
A⁻¹ is not computed entrywise: the inverse of [a b; c d] is NOT [1/a 1/b; 1/c 1/d]. Only diagonal matrices invert entrywise.

If AB = AC and A is invertible, then B = C.
Multiply on the left by A⁻¹.
A product of invertible n×n matrices is invertible.
If A is invertible, so is A + I.
Its inverse undoes the row operation.
If A is row equivalent to I, then A is invertible.

A free variable means a pivotless column.

cards.front: Entry (i, j) of AB? Size condition?

back.text: Row i of A dotted with column j of B. A m×n, B n×p ⇒ AB is m×p.
AB = [Ab₁ ⋯ Abₚ]: each column of AB is A times a column of B, a combination of A's columns.

cards.front: Three things that fail in matrix algebra?

back.text: AB = BA (fails in general); AB = AC ⇒ B = C (fails unless A invertible); AB = 0 ⇒ A = 0 or B = 0 (fails).
BᵀAᵀ and B⁻¹A⁻¹: both reverse the order.
Row reduce [A | I]. If you reach [I | B], B = A⁻¹; if A does not reduce to I, A is singular.

cards.front: Why does row reducing [A | I] produce A⁻¹?

back.text: The row operations are elementary matrices with Eₖ⋯E₁A = I, so Eₖ⋯E₁ = A⁻¹, and applying them to I gives A⁻¹.

cards.front: Solve AXB = C for X (A, B invertible).

back.text: X = A⁻¹CB⁻¹: left inverse on the left, right inverse on the right.

cards.front: What is an elementary matrix and what is its inverse?

back.text: I after one row operation; EA performs that operation on A. Its inverse is the elementary matrix of the reverse operation.

cards.front: A is invertible ⇔ … (in terms of elementary matrices)?

back.text: A is row equivalent to I ⇔ A is a product of elementary matrices.

cards.front: Five IMT conditions that fail together for singular A?

back.text: A not ~ I; fewer than n pivots; Ax = 0 has nontrivial solutions; columns dependent; columns don't span ℝⁿ; not one-to-one; not onto; det A = 0.

cards.front: Why does AB = I force BA = I for square matrices?

back.text: AB = I ⇒ Ax = b solvable for every b (x = Bb) ⇒ A invertible by the IMT ⇒ B = A⁻¹(AB) = A⁻¹ ⇒ BA = I.

cards.front: Does the IMT apply to non-square matrices?

back.text: No. E.g. A 3×2, B 2×3 can have BA = I₂ while AB (3×3) is always singular.

cards.front: If A² = A and A ≠ I, is A invertible?

back.text: No: multiplying by A⁻¹ would give A = I.

cards.front: If A³ − 2A + I = 0, what is A⁻¹?

back.text: A(2I − A²) = I, so A⁻¹ = 2I − A².

cards.front: Invertible linear transformation T(x) = Ax: inverse map?

back.text: S(x) = A⁻¹x, which exists iff A is invertible; then S(T(x)) = x and T(S(x)) = x.

cards.front: If AB is invertible (square), are A and B invertible?

back.text: Yes, both: det A · det B ≠ 0, or construct one-sided inverses.

prompt.text: . (a) For which h is A invertible? (b) For h = 3 find A⁻¹ by row reducing [A | I], and use it to solve Ax = (1, 0, 0).

solution.text: ; then R₃ − (h−1)R₂ leaves (h²−1) − 3(h−1) = (h−1)(h−2) in the corner. det = (h − 1)(h − 2). Invertible ⇔ h ≠ 1, 2.
Check one entry of AA⁻¹: row 3 of A (1, 3, 9) · column 1 (3, −5/2, 1/2) = 3 − 15/2 + 9/2 = 0 ✓.
What it tests: Rows 1, h, h² for nodes 1, 2, h form a Vandermonde matrix: singular exactly when two nodes coincide. Solving with A⁻¹e₁ is just reading a column.

prompt.text: Assume A, B, C, X are n×n and invertible. Solve for X: (B⁻¹XA)⁻¹ = CB. Then explain why “X = BC⁻¹A⁻¹ B⁻¹” type guesses fail.

solution.title: Solution
items: Invert a product in reverse order: (B⁻¹XA)⁻¹ = A⁻¹X⁻¹B.
So A⁻¹X⁻¹B = CB. Right-multiply by B⁻¹: A⁻¹X⁻¹ = C. Left-multiply by A: X⁻¹ = AC.
Check: A⁻¹X⁻¹B = A⁻¹(AC)B = CB ✓. Guesses fail because matrix multiplication isn’t commutative: you may only multiply both sides on the same side.

solution.text: What it tests: Two errors to avoid: (PQ)⁻¹ = P⁻¹Q⁻¹ (wrong order) and “cancelling” matrices that aren’t adjacent.

items: 1. If A is n×n and Ax = b has at least one solution for every b, then the columns of A are independent.
2. If A² = 0, then A is not invertible.
3. If A, B are n×n and AB is invertible, then A is invertible.
4. If A is 3×2 and B is 2×3, then AB can be invertible.
5. If A is invertible, then A + I is invertible.
6. (A + B)⁻¹ = A⁻¹ + B⁻¹ whenever all three inverses exist.
1. True. Onto ⇒ pivot in every row ⇒ (square) pivot in every column ⇒ independent columns. IMT.
2. True. If A⁻¹ existed, A = A⁻¹A² = 0, which is not invertible. (Or det(A)² = 0.)
3. True. det A · det B = det(AB) ≠ 0. Or: A·(B(AB)⁻¹) = I, and a one-sided inverse of a square matrix is two-sided.
4. False. ABx = 0 whenever Bx = 0, and B (2×3) has a nontrivial kernel. So AB (3×3) is singular. (BA, 2×2, can be invertible.)
5. False. A = −I: invertible, but A + I = 0.

solution.text: What it tests: The IMT applies only to square matrices. Non-square products like AB (3×3 from 3×2·2×3) are rank-limited.

hard.title: AB = 0 but BA ≠ 0

prompt.text: Find nonzero 2×2 matrices A, B with AB = 0 but BA ≠ 0. Explain why neither can be invertible.

hard.answer: e.g. A = [1 0; 0 0], B = [0 0; 1 0]; neither is invertible since that would force the other to be 0

solution.text: If A were invertible, B = A⁻¹(AB) = 0, contradiction. If B were invertible, A = (AB)B⁻¹ = 0, contradiction.
What it tests: Zero divisors exist among matrices; AB = 0 does not imply A = 0 or B = 0, and AB ≠ BA in general.

prompt.text: A is n×n with A³ − 2A + I = 0. Prove A is invertible and express A⁻¹ as a polynomial in A.

solution.title: Solution
items: Rearrange: I = 2A − A³ = A(2I − A²).
Also (2I − A²)A = 2A − A³ = I. So A is invertible with A⁻¹ = 2I − A². ∎
(Such matrices exist: the companion matrix of t³ − 2t + 1 satisfies the equation.)

solution.text: What it tests: Isolate I and factor out A. For square matrices one side suffices, but showing both is cleaner.

hard.title: Idempotent matrices are singular

prompt.text: Let A be n×n with A² = A and A ≠ I. Prove A is singular, and deduce Ax = 0 has a nontrivial solution.

hard.answer: A invertible would give A = I; nontrivial null vector x = Ay − y for any y with Ay ≠ y

solution.title: Solution
items: Suppose A invertible. Multiply A² = A by A⁻¹: A = I, contradiction. So A is singular.
IMT: singular ⇔ Ax = 0 has a nontrivial solution. Explicitly: pick y with Ay ≠ y (exists since A ≠ I); then x = Ay − y ≠ 0 and Ax = A²y − Ay = 0. ∎

solution.text: What it tests: Idempotent (projection) matrices other than I are never invertible — they collapse some direction.

solution.title: Solution
items: C − ABC = I, so this is I − BA + BA = I.
Square matrices: a right inverse is an inverse. ∎

prompt.text: invertible? For c = 0, find a nonzero vector in Nul A and a vector not in Col A.

hard.answer: Invertible iff c ∉ {0, ±√2}; at c = 0: (1, 0, −1) ∈ Nul A, (1, 0, 0) ∉ Col A

parsons.title: Inverse of a product
parsons.goal: Prove: if A and B are invertible n×n matrices, then AB is invertible and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.
lines: Also C(AB) = B⁻¹(A⁻¹A)B = B⁻¹IB = B⁻¹B = I.
So C is a two-sided inverse of AB.
Hence AB is invertible and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹. ∎

parsons.title: A one-sided inverse of a square matrix is two-sided
parsons.goal: Prove: if A, D are n×n and AD = I, then A is invertible and DA = I.
lines: Let b ∈ ℝⁿ. Then A(Db) = (AD)b = b, so Ax = b has a solution for every b.
So the columns of A span ℝⁿ, i.e. A has a pivot in every row.
A is square, so it has n pivots, and by the IMT A is invertible.
Multiply AD = I on the left by A⁻¹: D = A⁻¹.
distractors: So the columns of D are linearly independent, hence A = D.
Multiply AD = I on the right by A⁻¹: D = A⁻¹.
Therefore DA = AD since AD = I.

parsons.title: The inverse is unique
parsons.goal: Prove: an n×n matrix has at most one inverse.
lines: Suppose B and C both satisfy BA = AB = I and CA = AC = I.
distractors: Since AB = AC, cancel A to get B = C.
